name: Khoibu
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.quote: Uipo has a difference between major and minor syllables (following the terminology of Butler (2015)). Every lexical word requires at least one major syllable (there are some function words that do not) ... Minor syllables, on the other hand, are always open, and always have a short schwa as their vowel. Minor syllables do not seem to have contrastive tone, and no minimal pairs have been found. When words are elicited in isolation, the minor syllables are typically pronounced with a short falling contour. It is common to find words with a sesquisyllabic structure, that is, words consisting of a minor syllable followed by a major syllable ... There are four lexical tones.
new_statements.citation: Sæbø, Lilja Maria. 2021. Tone sandhi in Uipo. Himalayan Linguistics 20(2): 33-46. doi:10.5070/H920254000
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (16 pp., text layer). extracted text of PDF p.5 (journal p.35, §3 'Uipo phonology') contains the quoted passage word for word: 'Uipo has a difference between major and minor syllables (following the terminology of Butler (2015)). Every lexical word requires at least one major syllable (there are some function words that do not),... Minor syllables, on the other hand, are always open, and always have a short schwa as their vowel. Minor syllables do not seem to have contrastive tone[fn2], and no minimal pairs have been found. When words are elicited in isolation, the minor syllables are typically pronounced with a short falling contour. It is common to find words with a sesquisyllabic…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Uipo/Khoibu is described as a lexical tone language (four tones: high-falling 53, low-level 22, low-falling 41, high-level 44) whose words consist of toneless schwa 'minor' syllables and full 'major' syllables (at least one per lexical word, typically word-final in isolation); no source read makes any claim about word stress or accent, so prominence can only be inferred from the minor/major (sesquisyllabic) asymmetry, not from a stated stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (Tonal: checked syllables have an undetermined number of tones; minor syllables possibly tonal when derived from reduced Caː verb stems, fn.2.) L.B. Singh 2013/2015 and S.I. Singh 2016 analyse three tones instead of four; S.I. Singh 2016 states suprasegmentals comprise 'only tone' and 'no juncture'.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern lexical word phonology (isolation/elicited forms from Khangshim village speakers); Sæbø notes most lexical words end in a major syllable in isolation but may end in a minor-syllable suffix in context.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same variety: Uipo (endonym) = Khoibu (exonym), ISO nkb, Glottolog khoi1251, as spoken in Khangshim (Khamsing) village, Chandel district, Manipur; Sæbø, L.B. Singh and Schumann share the same principal consultant (Mosyel Syelsaangthyel Khaling), so the 3-tone vs 4-tone disagreement is analytical, not dialectal (Sæbø 2021 fn.5).

sources.citation: Sæbø, Lilja Maria. 2021. Tone sandhi in Uipo. Himalayan Linguistics 20(2): 33-46. doi:10.5070/H920254000
sources.quote: Uipo has a difference between major and minor syllables (following the terminology of Butler (2015)). Every lexical word requires at least one major syllable (there are some function words that do not) ... Minor syllables, on the other hand, are always open, and always have a short schwa as their vowel. Minor syllables do not seem to have contrastive tone, and no minimal pairs have been found. When words are elicited in isolation, the minor syllables are typically pronounced with a short falling contour. It is common to find words with a sesquisyllabic structure, that is, words consisting of a minor syllable followed by a major syllable ... There are four lexical tones.
sources.note: Nothing explicit on stress/accent. §3 (pp.34-36): 18 consonants, 5 vowels; words built from minor syllables (open, short schwa, no contrastive tone, 'short falling contour' in isolation) and major syllables (every lexical word needs at least one); sesquisyllabic minor+major common; four lexical tones on major syllables (53, 22, 41, 44); refers to Sæbø 2020 MA for sesquisyllabicity discussion.

TOC shows Ch.2 Phonology pp.28-57 with 2.2 Syllable structure (minor syllables p.39, major syllable p.41) and 2.5 Tones pp.49-57 (high/mid/low, tone spreading, tone sandhi); no stress or accent heading. Body text not readable anywhere online.

sources.citation: Schumann, Freya. 2023. Uipo tonology. Abstract, 26th Himalayan Languages Symposium (Paris, 4-6 Sept 2023), Book of abstracts p.59.
sources.note: Abstract only: adopts Sæbø's four-tone analysis, argues a 'fifth tone' allotone conditioned by syllable position and rhyme, low tone more stable under sandhi, 'phenomena at the boundary of prosody and tone'; no stress statement. Cites Bijenkumar Singh 2015 and Sæbø 2020, 2021.

sources.citation: Singh, Sagolsem Indrakumar. 2016. Phonological Systems of Khoibu. The Dawn Journal 5(1): 1209-1222.
sources.note: No stress statement; abstract: 'the study of suprasegmental includes only tone. Khoibu does not have juncture.' Three tones (level, falling, rising) with mono- and disyllabic contrast tables.

sources.citation: Singh, Laishram Bijenkumar. 2015. Khoibu Tone. Language in India 15(2): 29-42.
sources.note: No stress statement. Three tones (high/mid/low) with pitch tracks, syllable template (C)(C)V(C), tone spreading and three sandhi rules with pronominal prefixes; remarks that the first (prefixal Cə-) syllable of disyllables mostly bears level tone and that high-toned vowels are 'articulated with a greater force of breath'.

sources.citation: Singh, Laishram Bijenkumar. 2013. Sound System of Khoibu. Language in India 13(6): 496-506.
sources.note: No stress statement. Vowel/consonant inventory, clusters, syllable types, §1.7 Tone: 'Khoibu is a tonal language and there are three tones... rising, level and falling'; first syllable of disyllables mostly level tone.
